entities.name: Sewadjkare Hori
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sewadjkare Hori presided as a pharaoh of the late Thirteenth Dynasty, reigning over a fragmented Egypt for approximately five years, likely between 1648 and 1643 BCE, though some chronologies place his rule earlier, from 1669 to 1664 BCE. Emerging during the turbulent Second Intermediate Period, his brief tenure symbolizes the diminished authority of the central Egyptian state, which by this era had lost control over significant territories, particularly the Nile Delta to the Hyksos and the south to an ascendant Nubian kingdom. His reign is primarily attested through the Turin King List, a vital New Kingdom document, and a single scarab seal, underscoring the ephemeral nature of royal power during this transitional epoch.

Details of Sewadjkare Hori's reign remain largely obscure, a common predicament for many rulers of the late Thirteenth Dynasty. The Turin King List assigns him a regnal period of five years, a relatively substantial duration compared to the many ephemeral pharaohs who preceded and followed him in quick succession. While no monumental constructions or military campaigns can be definitively attributed to him, his continued presence on the throne for half a decade suggests a degree of stability, however localized, in the regions of Middle and Upper Egypt that remained under Theban control. His rule likely saw the continuation of administrative practices established by earlier Thirteenth Dynasty kings, focused on maintaining order and resource extraction within a shrinking dominion.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Sewadjkare Hori's five-year reign highlights the severe political fragmentation of Egypt during the Second Intermediate Period, contributing to the historical record of a weakened Thirteenth Dynasty preceding the Hyksos ascendancy. His obscurity reflects the diminished central authority before the eventual reunification under the New Kingdom.
